name: Multilingual and Code-Mixed Embeddings
question: Can one search serve Hindi, Hinglish and English?
summary: A multilingual embedding model maps English, Hindi in Devanagari and Roman-script Hinglish into one vector space, so “when will my refund arrive”, “पैसा कब आएगा” and “paisa kab aayega” land near the same English article. The work is choosing a model that covers your languages, normalising scripts before embedding, deciding whether to index translated copies, and measuring recall separately for each language. It builds on dense semantic embeddings; speech and voice input are a separate technique.
useCases: Customers write in Hindi, other Indian languages or Hinglish, but the help content is in English
Cross-lingual search: a Hindi query should find an English circular or policy
Any product whose overall search score looks fine but whose regional users complain

items.detail: e.g. BGE-M3, multilingual-e5, Cohere Embed multilingual: one space for about 100 languages
a Hindi query finds an English article with no translation step
Unicode NFC, then Roman Hindi transliterated to Devanagari
Hindi versions indexed beside English: more recall, twice the vectors
recall@5 for English, Hindi and Hinglish reported separately
Devanagari often needs more tokens per word than English

Compare a multilingual model with your English baseline on every language slice
Normalise Unicode and transliterate Roman Hindi before embedding queries
Add translated document copies only where a slice still falls short, then re-measure
pitfalls: An English-only model turns Devanagari into near-meaningless vectors
One overall recall number hides a failing language
Budgets and chunk sizes set on English undercount Hindi tokens

steps.title: One model for every language
steps.text: multilingual-e5-large maps about 100 languages, Hindi included, into one 1,024-dimension space. E5 models expect a “query: ” prefix on questions and a “passage: ” prefix on documents; skipping them quietly lowers recall.

steps.title: Know each query's language
steps.text: Devanagari is easy to spot from its Unicode block, U+0900 to U+097F. Hinglish is harder because it is plain ASCII; here two or more common Roman Hindi words mark it. In production a language-identification model does this job.

steps.title: Normalise before embedding
steps.text: Unicode NFC gives each Devanagari letter one byte form, so a nukta or vowel sign typed two ways embeds the same. Roman Hindi is then transliterated: “paisa kab aayega” becomes “पैसा कब आएगा”, while English words such as UPI stay as they are.

steps.title: Decide what goes in the index
steps.text: Kosh Bank, a fictional bank, has 2,40,000 English chunks. Adding a Hindi copy of each doubles the vectors to 4,80,000, and a Hindi chunk takes about 480 tokens against 300 for the English one, because Devanagari splits into more tokens.

steps.title: Search once, count each article once
steps.text: One search covers every language. Because an article and its Hindi copy can both score highly, the loop fetches 2k results and keeps the first hit per article id, so the top 5 holds five different articles.

steps.title: Measure every language slice
steps.text: Recall@5 is printed separately for English, Hindi and Hinglish. In the tuned setup that is 87%, 84% and 80%, so overall is 0.5 × 87 + 0.25 × 84 + 0.25 × 80 = 84.5%. With an English-only model the overall was 54.8%, which hid a Hindi slice at 8%.

pros: One index and one model serve English, Hindi and Hinglish
Hindi queries find English content with no translation step
Open models such as BGE-M3 and multilingual-e5 run on your own servers, which helps keep customer text in India
Per-language evaluation shows exactly which users are poorly served
cons: Multilingual models can score slightly lower on English than the best English-only model
Hinglish spelling varies widely, so normalisation is never perfect
Translated copies double the index and add a translation pass to maintain
Devanagari needs more tokens, so embedding and chunk budgets grow
avoidWhen: Every user and every document is in English (an English-only model may be a little better and smaller)
You cannot build a test set with real Hindi and Hinglish queries (measure first, or you will not know if it helped)

practice.scenario: Kosh Bank, a fictional bank, runs a support bot over 2,40,000 English help chunks. Half its customers write in English, a quarter in Hindi and a quarter in Hinglish such as “UPI fail hua, paisa kab aayega”. An English-only embedding model scored 54.8% recall@5 overall, which hid a Hindi slice at 8%. A multilingual model, transliteration of Roman Hindi and Hindi copies of the articles lift every language slice above 80%, and recall is now reported per language on every release.

industries.use: Hindi and Hinglish questions about UPI, cards and KYC answered from English help content
Policy wording in English retrieved for claims questions typed in Marathi, Tamil or Hinglish
Product search where shoppers mix scripts, such as “kurta cotton लाल”

practice.analogy: A multilingual reference librarian. Ask in Hindi, English or a mix of both and she walks to the same shelf, because she files books by what they are about, not by the language of the question. A new clerk who only reads English would send every Hindi question to the wrong aisle.

library.name: BGE-M3 with sentence-transformers
library.what: An open multilingual embedding model (1,024 dims, 100+ languages, inputs up to 8,192 tokens); sentence-transformers loads its dense vectors directly.

practice.note: The transliteration here is a tiny word lookup for illustration; in production use a transliteration model such as AI4Bharat IndicXlit, and a translation model such as IndicTrans2 for Hindi copies of articles. BGE-M3 needs no query prefix; multilingual-e5 models need “query: ” and “passage: ”.

samples.code:
import re, unicodedata
import numpy as np
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-m3")       # dense vectors, 1,024 dims

ROMAN_HINDI = {"paisa", "kab", "aayega", "kaise", "nahi", "mera", "karo", "hai", "kya", "wapas"}
LEXICON = {"paisa": "पैसा", "kab": "कब", "aayega": "आएगा", "wapas": "वापस",
           "mera": "मेरा", "kya": "क्या", "hai": "है", "nahi": "नहीं"}

def normalise(text: str) -> str:
    text = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text.strip())
    words = text.lower().split()
    if re.search(r"[ऀ-ॿ]", text) or len(set(words) & ROMAN_HINDI) < 2:
        return text                               # Devanagari or English: leave as typed
    return " ".join(LEXICON.get(w, w) for w in words)   # stub transliteration

articles = [
    ("A12", "Refunds for failed UPI payments reach your account within 5 working days."),
    ("A12", "विफल यूपीआई भुगतान का रिफंड 5 कार्यदिवसों में आपके खाते में आ जाता है।"),
    ("B07", "To block a lost debit card, open Cards and tap Block."),
]
ids = [a for a, _ in articles]
doc_vecs = model.encode([t for _, t in articles], normalize_embeddings=True)

def search(query: str, k: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    q = model.encode(normalise(query), normalize_embeddings=True)
    hits = []
    for i in np.argsort(-(doc_vecs @ q)):
        if ids[i] not in hits:                    # an article and its Hindi copy count once
            hits.append(ids[i])
    return hits[:k]

for q in ["when will my refund come", "पैसा कब आएगा", "upi fail hua paisa kab aayega"]:
    print(q, "->", search(q, k=1))

numericDrill.question: Kosh Bank indexes 2,40,000 English chunks of 300 tokens each and adds a Hindi translation of every chunk. Each Hindi chunk takes 1.6 times as many tokens as its English original. How many extra tokens, in millions, does embedding the Hindi copies add?
numericDrill.answer: Hindi chunk: 300 × 1.6 = 480 tokens. 2,40,000 × 480 = 11,52,00,000 tokens = 115.2 million, on top of the 72 million for the English chunks.

interview.question: How would you make an English help centre searchable in Hindi and Hinglish?
interview.answer: Use a multilingual embedding model such as BGE-M3 or multilingual-e5 so Hindi queries land near English articles. Normalise queries with Unicode NFC and transliterate Roman Hindi to Devanagari. Build a test set labelled by language from real chat logs, report recall@5 per slice, and add translated copies of the articles only where a slice still falls short.

interview.question: Why is a single overall recall figure dangerous for multilingual search?
interview.answer: It is a weighted average, so a large English slice can hide a failing smaller one. With 50% English at 88%, 25% Hindi at 8% and 25% Hinglish at 35%, overall is 54.8%, which looks mediocre rather than broken, yet Hindi users are almost never served. Always report each language separately.

mistakes.mistake: Embedding Hindi with an English-only model
mistakes.fix: Use a multilingual model and check it on a Hindi slice

mistakes.mistake: Treating Hinglish as English because it is ASCII
mistakes.fix: Detect Roman Hindi and transliterate it, or test that the model handles it as typed

quiz.question: A bank’s help articles are all in English. A customer asks “पैसा कब आएगा” and an English-only embedding model returns nothing useful. What is the most direct fix?
options: Switch to a multilingual embedding model so Hindi and English share one vector space
Add more English synonyms to the articles
quiz.explanation: An English-only model has almost no Hindi in its vocabulary, so Devanagari becomes near-meaningless vectors. A multilingual model places the Hindi query near the English article.

quiz.question: Queries are 50% English, 25% Hindi and 25% Hinglish. Recall@5 is 88%, 8% and 35%. What is overall recall@5?
Why is the 54.75% in the previous question a poor thing to put on a dashboard alone?
options: It hides that Hindi queries almost never find the right article
Hinglish should be excluded from evaluation
quiz.explanation: A weighted average lets the large English slice mask a failing Hindi slice at 8%. Report each language separately.

quiz.question: What does transliteration do to “paisa kab aayega”?
options: Translates it to “when will the money come”
Rewrites it in Devanagari as “पैसा कब आएगा”
quiz.explanation: Transliteration changes the script, not the language. Translation would change the language.

quiz.question: A normalise() function skips transliteration whenever query.isascii() is true. Which queries are handled wrongly?
options: Hinglish queries in Roman script, which are also ASCII
quiz.explanation: Roman Hindi is plain ASCII, so it is treated as English and never transliterated. Detect the language, not the character set.

quiz.question: An insurer indexes 1,50,000 English chunks and adds a Hindi copy of each, using a 1,024-dimension float32 model. How large is the raw vector index?
quiz.explanation: 3,00,000 vectors × 1,024 dims × 4 B = 1,228,800,000 B ≈ 1.23 GB. Without the copies it would be about 614 MB.

quiz.question: English chunks average 300 tokens and the Hindi translations take 1.6 times as many. How many tokens do 2,40,000 Hindi copies add?
Which are real multilingual embedding options as of 2026? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is an English sentence-transformers model. BGE-M3, multilingual-e5 and Cohere’s multilingual models cover about 100 languages.

quiz.question: A hospital uses intfloat/multilingual-e5-large but embeds queries and passages as raw text. What is likely wrong?
options: E5 expects “query: ” and “passage: ” prefixes; leaving them out lowers retrieval quality
quiz.explanation: E5 models were trained with these prefixes, and the model card asks for them. BGE-M3, by contrast, needs no query instruction.

quiz.question: Two copies of the same refund article, English and Hindi, both appear in a customer’s top 5. What should the search do?
options: Keep both, as they are different texts
De-duplicate by article id and fill the slot with the next distinct article
Drop the Hindi copy from the index
quiz.explanation: Fetch a few extra candidates and keep one hit per article id, so the top 5 holds five different answers.

quiz.question: A shopper types “लाल kurta cotton”. Which describes this query?
options: Code-mixed: Devanagari Hindi and Roman-script words in one query
quiz.explanation: Mixing scripts and languages within one query is common in India; the model and normalisation must handle both parts.

quiz.question: Kosh Bank’s Hinglish slice is at 58% with a multilingual model. Which steps are likely to raise it? Select all that apply.
options: Transliterate Roman Hindi to Devanagari before embedding
Add Hindi copies of the articles
Collect real Hinglish queries to test on
quiz.explanation: Transliteration and Hindi copies both helped in the playground (72% and 80%); real Hinglish test queries tell you whether they work on your data. An English-only model makes it worse.

quiz.question: Why do Hindi documents usually cost more to embed than English documents of the same meaning?
options: Devanagari usually splits into more tokens per word
Hindi text must be embedded twice
APIs charge more per Hindi token by rule
quiz.explanation: Tokenizers trained mostly on English break Devanagari into more pieces, so tokenizer fertility, and so cost and chunk length, rise.

quiz.question: A Hindi slice has 250 test queries and the right article appears in the top 5 for 210 of them. What is Hindi recall@5?
Hindi is 25% of traffic. Hindi recall rises from 74% to 84% while other slices stay the same. How much does overall recall rise?
Why apply Unicode NFC normalisation to Devanagari text before embedding?
options: So the same letter typed in two byte forms, such as a nukta letter, embeds the same way
quiz.explanation: Some Devanagari letters have precomposed and decomposed forms. NFC picks one, so identical-looking text gives identical input.

quiz.question: Which belong in a good multilingual retrieval test set? Select all that apply.
options: Real Hindi and Hinglish queries from logs, labelled by language
Several spellings of common Hinglish words, such as aayega and ayega
Only English queries machine-translated into Hindi
The correct article id for each query
quiz.explanation: Machine-translated English is cleaner than what customers type and misses code-mixing; use real queries with gold answers.

quiz.question: Which tool is built for transliterating Roman script into Indian scripts?
quiz.explanation: IndicXlit, trained on the Aksharantar dataset, transliterates between Roman script and 21 Indic languages.

quiz.question: A search index serves only English queries over English documents. Is a multilingual model worth it?
options: Usually not: an English-only model may be a little better and smaller
Always: multilingual models are better at English
Yes, because it halves the index size
Yes, because it removes the need for evaluation
quiz.explanation: Multilingual models spread capacity over many languages. With no other languages in play, compare both on your English queries.

quiz.question: Which statements about cross-lingual retrieval with a multilingual model are true? Select all that apply.
options: A Hindi query can find an English article with no translation step
Recall for Hindi queries is often lower than for English queries on English documents
Translated copies of documents can close part of the gap
It removes the need to evaluate each language
quiz.explanation: Cross-lingual matching works but usually trails same-language matching; translated copies help, and each language still needs its own evaluation.
